values.value: • Use your clear view of evaluation criteria to shape the proposal around what wins, not what is merely available. • Prioritise the top 3 to 5 buyer criteria in every conversation and document. • Bring proof against each criterion with evidence, references, and implementation clarity. • Check whether any criterion is weighted more heavily by the final approver. • Keep confirming that your current solution story matches their scorecard.
12|Strong
Buyer may say, 'Just show us the standard deck.' Response: 'I can, but I would rather spend time on the few points that matter most to your evaluation.'
Great. Build the proposal and demo around the exact evaluation points and show proof against each one.
Low risk. You can now sell to their scorecard.
Say: 'I will structure the next step around the criteria that matter most to your team.'
Strong

• Strengthen your understanding of how the buyer will judge options. • Ask what matters most between outcome, price, service, implementation, analytics, platform fit, or credibility. • Separate stated criteria from hidden decision drivers. • Tune demo and proposal around the high-weight items. • Move from adequate knowledge to a buyer-led win plan.
12|Adequate
Buyer may say, 'We are looking at multiple things.' Response: 'Understood. Which of those will really carry the most weight in the final decision?'
Deepen this. Adequate understanding still leaves room for competitor advantage if they know the hidden criteria better.
Risk: You may know the visible criteria, not the real ones.
Ask: 'Beyond price and features, what will make one option feel easier to approve?'
Adequate

• Do not keep presenting broad capability when the buyer's scorecard is unclear. • Ask directly how the final choice will be made and what would make one option stronger than another. • Listen for both formal criteria and real-world deciding factors. • Rework your pitch to answer the evaluation lens, not your standard deck. • Without this, you risk losing despite a good solution.
12|Weak
Buyer may say, 'We will know it when we see it.' Response: 'That happens often. It still helps me to know what would make one option feel clearly right from your side.'
Re-open discovery before polishing the pitch. A proposal built on weak criteria knowledge usually misses the mark.
High risk: Weak evaluation clarity.
Ask: 'What will the team use to judge fit, confidence, and readiness to move ahead?'
Weak

• This deal needs evaluation discovery before anything else becomes sharper. • Ask how the customer will compare vendors, what must be proven, and what the non-negotiables are. • Find out who owns the evaluation and whether different stakeholders value different things. • Do not guess their priorities from past deals. • The more you know here, the less random the outcome becomes.
12|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'Just share everything.' Response: 'I can, though it will be far more useful if I know how you plan to compare and choose.'
Do not submit a polished answer to an unknown test. First learn how they will evaluate this opportunity.
High risk: You do not know how they will choose.
Ask: 'What are the top decision criteria and who owns each of them internally?'
Don't know
Your understanding of the evaluation criteria of the customer for this opportunity?
